findings.detail: Terms carrying decisive weight are used without definition or forward reference: 'lane', 'run generation', 'effective authority', 'overlay', 'admitted', 'Detector Reviewer', 'Corpus Builder', 'Oracle Curator', 'static prior', 'canary registry', 'auxiliary corpus', 'intention-to-treat', 'INVALID_HARNESS', 'composite', 'held-out functional component', 'schema-blind'. Several are used in dispositive sentences ('anything not enumerated is inaccessible', 'a positive control proves denial') where misunderstanding changes what a reader would do. The amendment cannot be read standalone even though it is the document a founder is being asked to ratify.
findings.evidence: Section 2.6: 'the schema-blind Oracle Curator as the strongest competent questions available from pre-change evidence' — 'schema-blind', 'pre-change evidence', and the Curator's existence are all introduced in the same clause with no definition. Section 2.3 names 'Corpus Builder snapshot map, static prior, Oracle Curator census/draw, gold calibration set' as things that 'do not exist yet' without ever saying what any of them are.
findings.recommendation: Either add a short glossary appendix defining the ~20 load-bearing role and artifact nouns, or add a one-line 'defined in spec/X.md §Y' pointer at first use of each. At minimum define: lane, run generation, effective authority, admitted, positive control, composite vs functional score, and each named non-obvious role (Detector Reviewer, Oracle Curator, Corpus Builder).

findings.title: The old-block/new-block overlay format gives no way to verify anchor uniqueness before submitting for ratification
findings.detail: The mechanism is stated ('each exact old block below must occur once in the base artifact... A missing, duplicate, or mismatched anchor is AUTHORITY_MISMATCH and blocks both author lanes'), but there is no tooling, no command, no file format, and no ordering rule given. A user cannot check their own amendment for anchor errors before it reaches the gate; they discover failure at G-1 with a single opaque code and no indication of which of the ~14 blocks failed or why. Whitespace, blockquote-marker, and line-wrapping normalization are unspecified — the document itself contains blocks that are re-wrapped in the source (e.g. the V-10 co-primary paragraph ends mid-sentence with 'feed a'), so it is not obvious what 'exact' means.
findings.evidence: Section 2.6: 'In spec/verification.md V-10 replace this exact old co-primary paragraph: > ... The pilot covariance and one-sided 90% upper variance bounds feed a' — the quoted old block ends mid-sentence, and the new block also ends 'feed a'. A reader cannot tell whether the trailing partial sentence is intentional (partial-paragraph replacement) or a transcription error, and there is no stated normalization rule to resolve it.
findings.recommendation: Specify exactly one normalization rule (e.g. 'blockquote markers stripped, trailing whitespace stripped, line breaks normalized to a single space, then byte-compared'), give each replacement block a stable ID (R-1..R-14), require AUTHORITY_MISMATCH to name the failing block ID and whether the cause was zero/multiple matches, and provide or name a dry-run command that reports all anchor resolutions before ratification.

findings.title: Error codes appear without a catalog: no reader can tell what to do next when one fires
findings.detail: Nine distinct terminal/blocking codes appear across the document — AUTHORITY_MISMATCH, FACTORY_QUESTION, UNFUNDED, INVALID_RUN, INVALID_HARNESS, NOT_PROVEN, PRODUCT_FAILURE, AUTHORITY_ONLY_COMPLETE_ORACLE, UNFUNDED_OR_UNDERPOWERED, INCONCLUSIVE_CEILING. Some are defined in place, some are defined nowhere in this document ('the existing INVALID_RUN disposition'), and none are collected. Their relationships are unclear: is NOT_PROVEN recoverable? Does INVALID_HARNESS require a new amendment, a new Tester, or just a rerun? Does UNFUNDED permanently end the route or pause it? A user hitting one of these has no place to look up what happens next.
findings.evidence: Section 2.6: 'Curator failure or discretionary post-output revision is INVALID_HARNESS' — no statement of what INVALID_HARNESS obligates. Section 2.2: 'a measurement-time host or unbound runtime change has the existing INVALID_RUN disposition' — defers to an unnamed prior document.
findings.recommendation: Add a table: code | raised by | meaning | who owns remediation | is the run recoverable | does it require a new amendment. Even a five-column table of ten rows would make the failure surface navigable.

findings.title: Budget arithmetic is stated as conclusions with no shown derivation, so a reader cannot check or reproduce it
findings.detail: The gate is 'a 30-minute cold-load allowance (USD 17.01 at the current rate), five full warm Coder hours, and a USD 22.01 reserve.' At the stated USD 34.0022/hour, five warm hours is USD 170.01, so the admission threshold is 17.01 + 170.01 + 22.01 = USD 209.03 — but that number is never written. Separately the monitor 'warns the founder by USD 210 cumulative spend'; against a starting balance of ~300 and reported remaining 246.4946, cumulative spend is ~53.52, so the 210 warn and the ~209 admission floor are measured in opposite directions (spend vs remaining balance) and sit suspiciously close numerically. A reader has to reconstruct all of this to know whether the numbers cohere, and 'the current rate' is not pinned to a specific figure at the point of use.
findings.evidence: Section 2.5: 'must cover a 30-minute cold-load allowance (USD 17.01 at the current rate), five full warm Coder hours, and a USD 22.01 reserve.' The sum is never stated; the rate is only given earlier as an observation, not as the operative constant.
findings.recommendation: State the admission inequality explicitly with a worked example: 'conservative_remaining >= 17.01 + (5 x hourly_rate) + 22.01; at the observed 34.0022/hr this is USD 209.03.' Add a small worked table of the four monitor thresholds (warn 210 spend, per-turn denial, stop 285, destroy 295) alongside their equivalent remaining-balance values so the two accounting frames are visibly reconciled.

findings.title: G-5 is marked optional in prose but the table's failure disposition reads like a penalty
findings.detail: The gate table gives G-5's failure disposition as 'omit the prior tree entirely', which reads as a consequence. Only in the trailing paragraph does the reader learn 'G-5 is optional: omitting all Python prior art satisfies it.' These are the same outcome described once as a failure and once as a pass, 800 words apart. A reader working the table top-to-bottom would treat G-5 as a blocker they must clear.
findings.evidence: Table row G-5 failure disposition: 'omit the prior tree entirely'. Closing paragraph: 'G-5 is optional: omitting all Python prior art satisfies it.'
findings.recommendation: Add an 'Optional?' column to the gate table, or restate G-5's disposition as 'not a blocker; the route proceeds with no prior art'. Mark every optional gate the same way.

findings.title: Gate table does not encode ordering or concurrency, which is stated only in a preceding sentence
findings.detail: 'Coder and Tester may run concurrently only after G-1 through G-4 pass' is the sole statement of sequencing, and it is prose above a table that otherwise looks like a linear checklist. The table cannot answer: can G-5 run before G-2? Must G-8 complete before G-6 starts, or only before G-9? Is G-10 blocked on G-9? A reader planning execution has to infer the dependency graph from role names and inference.
findings.evidence: Section 8 preamble: 'Coder and Tester may run concurrently only after G-1 through G-4 pass.' The table has columns Gate | Owner | Required evidence | Failure disposition — no 'depends on' column.
findings.recommendation: Add a 'Prerequisites' column naming the gates each row depends on, and note which rows may run in parallel. A two-line ASCII dependency sketch above the table would also do it.

findings.title: Section 2.6's proof-gate corrections are unrelated to the stated problem and arrive with no transition
findings.detail: Sections 0-2.5 are about Rust and the Vast host. Section 2.6 abruptly introduces four statistical/measurement changes (abstention floors, a competent authority-only comparator, co-primary functional endpoints, egress hold-back) and a records-retention change. The heading says 'discovered before any pilot' and the body says they 'repair pre-outcome falsifiability', but nothing explains why these are bundled into a language-and-hosting amendment rather than a separate one. A reader evaluating whether to ratify has to decide on two logically independent bundles as one unit and is given no rationale for the coupling.
findings.evidence: Section 1 Problem statement mentions only Python/Ollama failure and the founder's Rust preference. Section 2.6 introduces 'the lower 95% paired bound on full-system - authority-only composite is at least 0.10' — an endpoint change with no connection to language or host.
findings.recommendation: Add one or two sentences at the head of 2.6 explaining the coupling (e.g. 'these are bundled because ratification creates a fresh Factory generation and a new Tester instrument, which is the only point at which the instrument can be changed without discarding admitted work'). If no such reason exists, split into a second amendment.

findings.title: Unstated behavior when a replacement anchor is itself modified by another replacement in this amendment
findings.detail: Multiple replacements target spec/verification.md V-10, and one insert-after targets an 'intention-to-treat block' in the same section. If any new block introduced by an earlier replacement contains text matching a later anchor, or if two anchors overlap, the outcome is undefined. The document says only that each anchor must occur once in the base artifact — it does not say whether anchors are resolved against the base or against the partially-overlaid artifact, nor whether replacement order matters.
findings.evidence: Section titled 'It supersedes only the clauses named below' plus multiple V-10 replacements and one V-10 insert-after, with no stated application order.
findings.recommendation: State explicitly: 'All anchors resolve against the unmodified base artifact; replacements are applied atomically; overlapping anchor spans are AUTHORITY_MISMATCH.' Then the reader knows the semantics without experimenting.

findings.title: Ambiguous plural in the balance/reserve rule when rate changes mid-run
findings.detail: The monitor 'recomputes all reserves at the greater observed/current rate' and 'a price or host change closes the next-turn gate until rebound.' But the pre-restart admission uses 'the current rate' fixed at 34.0022/hr, and the fixed dollar figures (17.01, 22.01) were derived from that rate. If the rate rises after admission, it is unclear whether the dollar constants recompute (17.01 -> new_rate/2) or stay fixed while only the five-hour term scales. A user watching the monitor cannot predict when the next-turn gate closes.
findings.evidence: Section 2.5: '(USD 17.01 at the current rate)' fixes a dollar figure derived from a rate, then later 'recomputes all reserves at the greater observed/current rate'.
findings.recommendation: Express the reserve terms as formulas in the rate rather than as dollar constants: 'cold-load allowance = 0.5 x rate; reserve = 0.5 x rate + 5.00'. Then the recomputation rule is unambiguous and the sampled dollar values become illustrative.

findings.title: External source citation lacks a retrieval artifact
findings.detail: The document cites 'docs.vast.ai/guides/instances/connect/ssh, observed 2026-09-05' as evidence for a security-relevant claim (Vast supplies no separate host-key attestation). A reader cannot verify this later if the page changes; there is no archived copy digest, unlike every other fact in the document which is content-addressed.
findings.evidence: Section 2.2: '(docs.vast.ai/guides/instances/connect/ssh, observed 2026-09-05)'
findings.recommendation: Record a SHA-256 of the retrieved page bytes in the run ledger alongside the URL and date, consistent with the amendment's own treatment of every other external observation.

findings.title: No index or cross-reference between the failure-mode list, the constraints list, and the gate table
findings.detail: Failure modes (section 3, 13 items), constraints (section 4, 14 bullets), and gates (section 8, 11 rows) largely restate the same obligations in three formats. A reader cannot tell which failure mode is enforced by which gate, so it is impossible to check coverage — e.g. failure mode 13 (named-human rights grant) maps to G-8, but failure mode 6 (ambiguous mutation state) maps to G-4 only by inference.
findings.evidence: Failure mode 6: 'A response/tool interruption produces ambiguous mutation state...' vs G-4 required evidence: '...mid-forwarding/mutating-tool recovery drills'. The correspondence is real but never stated.
findings.recommendation: Add a gate reference (G-n) to each failure mode and each constraint bullet. This is a low-cost change that makes the three lists mutually navigable and reveals any orphaned obligation.

persona_reports.summary: This document is rigorous but unnavigable by anyone who is not already inside the project: it opens with digests and overlay mechanics rather than a plain statement of what changes, uses roughly twenty undefined load-bearing nouns, and scatters ten error codes with no catalog of what each obliges. The most actionable fixes are cheap — a summary block, a glossary, an error-code table, prerequisite and optional columns on the gate table, and gate references on the failure-mode and constraint lists. The one substantive design gap is the overlay mechanism itself: `AUTHORITY_MISMATCH` is a single opaque code for fourteen anchor replacements with no stated normalization rule and no dry-run path, and at least one quoted anchor block ends mid-sentence, which a first-time reader cannot tell is intentional.

findings.title: Rust 1.98.1 / edition 2024 pin and the quoted channel-manifest digest are not verifiable facts
findings.detail: The amendment pins `rust-toolchain.toml` to Rust 1.98.1 with edition 2024 and asserts a specific SHA-256 for `channel-rust-1.98.1.toml`. Rust's release cadence is six weeks from 1.0 (2015-05-15); 1.98 would land around mid-2027 on that schedule, and the rest of the document dates itself to 2026-09. Edition 2024 stabilized in 1.85, so that part is coherent, but the version number is either a future/hypothetical release or a typo for 1.89.x/1.9x. More seriously, a 64-hex digest for a channel manifest is exactly the kind of value that must be *observed*, not authored — and the document elsewhere is scrupulous about distinguishing observation from assertion (§2.5 records the exact Vast balance with a timestamp; §2.2 records the vLLM manifest digest). This one digest appears with no observation receipt, no `rustup` download record, and no date. Under the amendment's own G-1 anchor discipline, an unverifiable pinned digest is an `AUTHORITY_MISMATCH` waiting to happen at build time, and it will block the Coder lane after the expensive host is already warm and burning USD 34/hour.
findings.evidence: "Rust is pinned by `rust-toolchain.toml` to 1.98.1. The official channel manifest `channel-rust-1.98.1.toml` has SHA-256 `a7c8774a5fd8441c997d94c029776cbc5eb111e9d72ab5d256fa69866644347e`;"
findings.recommendation: Either (a) attach a dated Validator observation receipt for the toolchain exactly as §2.5 does for the Vast balance, including `rustup` fetch time, mirror URL, and `rustc -Vv`, or (b) state the pin as `<toolchain to be pinned at G-4 by observed manifest digest>` and make toolchain observation an explicit G-4 sub-gate. Do not ship an authored-looking digest into an append-only authority artifact.

findings.title: The lineage-first egress gate is asserted but its lineage source-of-truth is never specified, and it cannot be built as described
findings.detail: The document repeatedly makes the lineage gate load-bearing: it 'admits only the ratified Coder prompt and tool results produced from readable Coder-lane roots, rejects any Personal/Company/Tester/Oracle/secret/forbidden-marker lineage, then byte-scans as defense in depth' and records 'source-event IDs'. But a Codex harness emits an opaque request body — a JSON array of messages assembled from model-authored text, tool call arguments the *model* wrote, and tool results. There is no described mechanism by which a byte in a tool result is tagged with a provenance label that survives concatenation, summarization, or model paraphrase. The model can trivially launder a forbidden byte by reading it in one turn and re-emitting it as its own prose in the next; that prose has 'model' lineage, not 'Personal' lineage, and passes the lineage check. The byte-scan is then the *only* real control, which contradicts the framing of byte-scanning as mere 'defense in depth'. This matters because §3 failure mode 4 and G-3 treat an unauthorized send as permanently route-blocking and irreversible.
findings.evidence: "The gate admits only the ratified Coder prompt and tool results produced from readable Coder-lane roots, rejects any Personal/Company/Tester/Oracle/secret/forbidden-marker lineage, then byte-scans as defense in depth. It records request digest, byte count, authorized purpose, source-event IDs, and decision before forwarding."
findings.recommendation: Specify the lineage mechanism concretely: (1) the gate's authority is the OS sandbox — if the Coder process literally cannot open a Personal/Tester path, no tool result can carry those bytes, so lineage reduces to *capability* enforcement plus a per-tool-call read manifest; (2) state explicitly that model-authored text has unbounded lineage and is therefore covered only by the byte-scan and the sandbox, not by lineage tagging. Reorder the stated defense: capability confinement is primary, byte-scan is secondary, 'lineage' is a bookkeeping receipt over tool-call read manifests. As written the ordering overclaims.

findings.title: Disabling vLLM prefix cache persistence does not make prefix state 'volatile' in the sense claimed
findings.detail: §2.2 permits prefix caching on the grounds that 'repo-derived prefixes are transient memory inside the explicitly authorized Coder processor boundary'. In vLLM, the prefix cache is GPU HBM (and, if CPU offload is enabled — which the doc correctly disables) host RAM. But the amendment also allows the instance to be *stopped* with its 1 TB disk retained for up to six hours (§2.5). vLLM v0.28 with `--enable-prefix-caching` does not persist to disk by default, so the specific claim holds for the running server; however the broader inference that 'volatile' implies 'not recoverable by the host operator' is false while the process is live — a host operator with root can read process memory and GPU memory. The document acknowledges the host-operator threat elsewhere ('container isolation is not a confidentiality proof') but the prefix-cache paragraph reads as if volatility were a mitigation. It is a persistence mitigation only, not a confidentiality one.
findings.evidence: "prefix caching is permitted because repo-derived prefixes are transient memory inside the explicitly authorized Coder processor boundary after ratification. It is volatile provider state, not public-only state, not a result journal, not recovery evidence, and not part of any correctness claim"
findings.recommendation: Add one clause: 'Volatility bounds accidental persistence across restart; it does not exclude the host operator, who is already covered by the §2.4 residual.' Also state explicitly that the instance is destroyed rather than stopped if any repository-bearing request has occurred, or accept that stopped-with-disk-retained is a distinct custody state and record it in the residual.

findings.title: The `authority-only` arm is now co-primary, which converts a mechanism control into a success gate the amendment elsewhere denies
findings.detail: §2.6 replaces the old paragraph that explicitly said 'authority-only is a mechanism-attribution control, not a hidden success gate' with one making a 0.10 lower-bound over authority-only a co-primary conjunct. That is a legitimate strengthening, but it interacts badly with the Oracle Curator instruction to 'maximize—not handicap—the authority-only control'. The stronger the Curator makes the comparator, the more likely the conjunction fails for reasons unrelated to whether the maintained corpus works — specifically, the Curator has discretion over 'the strongest competent questions available from pre-change evidence', and 'strongest' is undefined and unbounded above. There is no ceiling rule analogous to `AUTHORITY_ONLY_COMPLETE_ORACLE` (which only excludes tasks where the replies contain the *complete* oracle). A Curator maximizing under a fixed budget can plausibly land at 'nearly complete oracle' repeatedly, making the 0.10 margin unattainable by construction while every task remains individually eligible. The amendment's own §5.7 admits this risk but treats it only as 'may require larger N', when the real risk is a systematic, N-invariant ceiling.
findings.evidence: "the lower 95% paired bound on `full-system - authority-only` composite is at least 0.10, establishing maintained-corpus value beyond direct authority consultation;" combined with "instructed to maximize—not handicap—the authority-only control under a fixed time/tool/call budget"
findings.recommendation: Preregister the fixed authority-only budget (max calls, max reply bytes, max wall time) as an explicit numeric constant in the amendment rather than leaving 'fixed' undefined, and preregister a pilot-observable eligibility rule: if pilot authority-only composite exceeds some preregistered value, the task family is `AUTHORITY_ONLY_NEAR_ORACLE` and excluded before draw. Otherwise the Curator's discretion is an unfalsifiable knob on a co-primary endpoint, which is the exact failure the section claims to repair.

findings.title: Ten co-primary conjuncts at alpha 0.05 each with paired bootstrap bounds is very likely underpowered at any fundable N
findings.detail: The new V-10 paragraph enumerates roughly ten co-primary endpoints (absolute composite 0.90; absolute functional 0.90; two ±0.05 TOST equivalences; two 0.15 lifts; four-to-five 0.10 superiorities; plus a restricted-stratum triple). Intersection-union testing is statistically correct — no alpha adjustment needed, each null tested at 0.05 — but joint power is the product-ish of marginal powers under correlation. With ~10 conjuncts each requiring, say, 85% marginal power, joint power is well under 30% unless the endpoints are strongly positively correlated. TOST equivalence at ±0.05 on a composite is particularly expensive: equivalence bounds narrower than the noise floor typically need several times the N of a superiority test at the same effect. The document requires 'joint power rules' and says failure is `UNFUNDED_OR_UNDERPOWERED`, which is honest, but §5.7 frames it as a mere possibility rather than the likely default. Given the founder has USD 300 for the Coder alone and V-10 measurement is separately funded, there is a real concept risk that the amendment as ratified is unprovable-by-construction and everyone discovers it after the Coder budget is spent.
findings.evidence: "Co-primary endpoints are absolute full-system composite quality 0.90; absolute full-system held-out functional quality 0.90; full-system composite and functional equivalence to their oracle-spec values within ±0.05; paired composite lift over baseline 0.15 and `null-system` 0.15; paired composite superiority over `static-prior`, `distractor`, each top-k control, and competent `authority-only` 0.10; paired superiority over `codebase-only` ... and authorization-restricted-stratum quality/lift/equivalence at the same 0.90/0.15/±0.05 bounds."
findings.recommendation: Move the joint-power feasibility check *before* G-6, not after. A cheap desk simulation with plausible variance/covariance priors costs nothing and can be run today; if it shows joint power under (say) 50% at any N the founder could plausibly fund, the endpoint set should be renegotiated now rather than after the Rust build. Add an explicit G-0 'endpoint set is jointly attainable in principle' analytic gate.

findings.title: GLM-5.3 / GLM-4.7 / vLLM v0.28 / zai-org revision are asserted as existing artifacts with no observation receipt for the model repo
findings.detail: The document pins a model repository revision, a container manifest digest, and two named parser plugins ('GLM-4.7 tool parser', 'GLM-4.5 reasoning parser'). The vLLM image is given a manifest digest, which is verifiable. The model repo is given a git revision, which is verifiable. But nowhere is there a receipt stating *when* these were resolved and by whom, in contrast to the meticulous Vast balance observation with a UTC timestamp. §5.1 says the pinned model/runtime 'sustained a 262,067-input-token synthetic request', which implies observation, but the artifact list itself carries no observation metadata. Separately, the amendment names a 755.7 GB FP8 checkpoint and a 1 TB retained disk — that is a 74% fill with runtime image, KV overhead, and logs also resident. That margin is thin enough to be a launch-gate risk and is not called out.
findings.evidence: "model repository `zai-org/GLM-5.3` at Git revision `aca966e4e02791568aa6a4ced368624b3d897f42`; official native-FP8 model files (approximately 755.7 GB)" and "instance `50012413` stopped with its 1 TB disk retained"
findings.recommendation: Attach the resolution timestamp and observer to the model/image block exactly as §2.5 does for balance. Add an explicit disk-headroom check to G-2: required free bytes after model + image + expected logs, with a named margin, because a mid-run ENOSPC on a USD 34/hour host is an expensive and entirely foreseeable failure.

findings.title: The Kindex `kin` CLI dependency reintroduces a Python interpreter into the deployed system despite the 'no Python in production paths' claim
findings.detail: §2.1 states 'Production paths contain no Python interpreter or Python package dependency.' §2.2 and §6 then require that adapters 'invoke the absolute, startup-verified, manifest-pinned `kin` executable' and that 'The Rust binary still depends operationally on the separately installed, pinned Kindex `kin` CLI'. Kindex is described as 'the existing Kindex package' with 'Kindex SQLite internals' and prior text called it a Python package. The two statements are reconciled only by a narrow reading of 'production paths' as 'the Kinbase build artifact', which is a packaging distinction, not a deployment or threat-surface one. §6 makes the right disclosure, but §2.1's flat assertion will be read as authority and could be cited to reject a correct implementation.
findings.evidence: "Production paths contain no Python interpreter or Python package dependency." vs. "The Rust binary still depends operationally on the separately installed, pinned Kindex `kin` CLI for Personal/legacy Codebase compatibility"
findings.recommendation: Reword §2.1 to 'The Kinbase build artifact and its first-party dependency graph contain no Python interpreter or Python package dependency; the externally installed Kindex `kin` CLI remains an operational subprocess dependency per §2.2 and §6.' One sentence, removes the contradiction.

findings.title: `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` plus 'no first-party unsafe' plus mandatory `fexecve`/Landlock/macOS-sandbox is a real feasibility cliff that is assumed away too cheaply
findings.detail: §5.2 correctly labels this 'load-bearing feasibility risk'. But the specific primitives named are uneven in ecosystem support: Landlock has a maintained safe crate; `fexecve`/`execveat` and descriptor enumeration are covered by `nix`/`rustix` safe-ish wrappers; macOS `sandbox_init` is deprecated by Apple, undocumented, and has no maintained safe crate with the audit posture this document demands ('version- and checksum-pinned', 'dependency source/function inventory and audit'). The likely outcome is a `FACTORY_QUESTION` on macOS specifically, mid-run, after the budget clock has started. That is the designed behavior, but it is a predictable stall on a USD 34/hour host.
findings.evidence: "Maintained, version- and checksum-pinned syscall crates may encapsulate platform `fstat`, descriptor closing, `fexecve`/`execveat`, Landlock, and macOS sandbox primitives behind narrow Kinbase-owned interfaces." and "If the platform boundary cannot be met through audited safe APIs, the Coder returns `FACTORY_QUESTION` and stops."
findings.recommendation: Resolve the macOS sandbox crate question *before* G-4 as a desk exercise (it costs nothing and no GPU time): name the specific crate and version, or pre-authorize the narrow exception in this amendment with its audit conditions, or scope the first proof to Linux/Landlock only. Discovering this at authoring time converts a five-minute research task into an hour of GPU spend plus a re-ratification cycle.

findings.title: The 15-minute checkpoint watchdog and the 30-minute forced turn cancellation can deadlock a long turn
findings.detail: The spend monitor 'forcibly cancels a turn at 30 minutes'. The watchdog requires a checkpoint every 15 minutes and 'a missed watchdog interval blocks the next model turn until a checkpoint is made'. A single model turn that runs 25 minutes will cross one watchdog interval with the Coder mid-generation and no new commit; the watchdog snapshots dirty work via a private temp index, which is fine, but the interaction between 'blocks the next model turn' and 'forcibly cancels at 30 minutes' is unspecified when the cancellation itself is what produces the dirty state. Minor, but it is a live-lock shape in a system where each blocked minute costs USD 0.57.
findings.evidence: "a Validator watchdog snapshots dirty work at least every fifteen minutes ... A missed watchdog interval blocks the next model turn until a checkpoint is made" and "forcibly cancels a turn at 30 minutes"
findings.recommendation: State the precedence explicitly: the watchdog snapshot is non-blocking and runs concurrently with an in-flight turn; only a *failed* snapshot blocks the next turn. And state that a forced 30-minute cancellation always triggers an immediate snapshot before the block is evaluated.

findings.title: The append-only deterministic-overlay amendment mechanism is well-constructed and should be preserved
findings.detail: The exact-old-block / exact-new-block overlay with once-only anchor matching and `AUTHORITY_MISMATCH` on duplicate or missing anchors is a sound design — it is essentially a content-addressed patch with a fail-closed application semantics, and it correctly refuses to produce a 'readable merged spec' that could diverge from the receipts. The refusal to rewrite the base manifest (Alternative 6) is the right call and is consistent with how signed-artifact supersession works in practice. Noting this so the review record shows it was examined and endorsed, not merely unremarked.
findings.evidence: "each exact **old** block below must occur once in the base artifact and is replaced by the paired exact **new** block; an **insert-after** instruction must find its exact anchor once. ... A missing, duplicate, or mismatched anchor is `AUTHORITY_MISMATCH` and blocks both author lanes."
findings.recommendation: No change. Consider only adding that anchor matching is byte-exact including whitespace and line endings, since several anchors span multiple lines with wrapping that could be reflowed by an editor.

persona_reports.summary: **Summary:** This is unusually disciplined work — the observation/assertion separation, the intention-to-treat and hold-back-never-scrub rules, the custody residual, and the append-only overlay mechanism are all things I'd defend in review. My blocking concerns are narrower than the document's length suggests: the Rust 1.98.1 pin and its channel-manifest digest appear authored rather than observed and violate the document's own evidentiary standard, and the "lineage-first, byte-scan as defense in depth" ordering overclaims what lineage tagging can do against a model that can paraphrase any byte it reads. Beyond that, I'd want the joint-power feasibility of ten co-primary conjuncts and the macOS-sandbox-without-unsafe question settled as free desk exercises *before* the USD 34/hour clock starts, because both are predictable stalls that will otherwise be discovered at the worst possible moment. Fix the toolchain receipt and the lineage framing and I'd sign off.

findings.title: The $300 budget cannot fund the thing it's supposed to fund, and the document already says so
findings.detail: You've spent $53.52 to get a model loaded. $246 remains. At $34/hr that's ~7.25 gross hours, and the gate requires 30min cold load ($17) + 5 warm hours ($170) + $22 reserve = $209 committed before a single repository-bearing request. That leaves ~$37 of slack for everything that goes wrong. Meanwhile the deliverable is a full Rust rewrite of a 29-module system that must satisfy P-1 through P-10, macOS sandboxing, Landlock/bubblewrap, descriptor enumeration, fexecve, non-convertible store handles, forbid(unsafe_code), signed .kin/ protocol, SQLite Company service, and a Kindex subprocess adapter layer. That is not a five-hour job for a human team, let alone a single model turn stream with a 30-minute per-turn cap. The document's own Assumption 3 admits 'Seven gross hours is not evidence that a complete candidate will exist.' You have written a very careful document about how to honorably fail. The probability-weighted outcome here is: you spend $246 and get UNFUNDED with no admissible commit — the eighth consecutive termination without a Coder commit.
findings.evidence: §2.5: 'Before restart, the Validator's conservative remaining-dollar figure must cover a 30-minute cold-load allowance (USD 17.01...), five full warm Coder hours, and a USD 22.01 reserve'. §1: 'terminated seven times without an admissible Coder commit'. §6: 'Seven available GPU-hours may end without an admissible commit.' G-6 requires 'one clean Rust commit covering every P-1 through P-10 implementation surface'.
findings.recommendation: Before spending another dollar, do a paper estimate: how many tokens of Rust does P-1..P-10 require? At what tokens/sec on this config? What's the realistic turn count? If the number says 40 hours, then $300 is not a budget, it's a donation. Either raise the ceiling to a number that matches the work, or explicitly reframe this run as 'buy information about whether the Coder can make progress at all' with a defined partial-progress success criterion — not 'complete P-1 through P-10 or nothing.' The current framing guarantees a zero.

findings.title: All-or-nothing G-6 makes every dollar spent worthless unless the last one succeeds
findings.detail: G-6 has exactly two states: complete Rust commit covering every P-1..P-10 surface, or 'incomplete/blocked Coder result; never a milestone.' Alternative 7 explicitly rejects a vertical slice. This means the payoff function is a step function at the very end of a budget you already know is marginal. Financially this is the worst possible structure: you get zero salvage value from 90% completion. If the Coder produces 8,000 lines of clean, boundary-correct Rust and runs out of money on P-9, the document says you have nothing. That's not rigor, that's a design that converts partial success into total loss.
findings.evidence: G-6 failure disposition: 'incomplete/blocked Coder result; never a milestone.' §7 Alternative 7: 'Build a smaller vertical slice inside the remaining budget: rejected because it would test code shape rather than the founder's complete P-1 through P-10 concept.'
findings.recommendation: Separate 'is this an admissible Product proof candidate' (correctly all-or-nothing) from 'is this code worth keeping and building on' (should not be). Define a checkpoint artifact that survives an UNFUNDED outcome: the worktree at last checkpoint, with its digest and provenance, retained as unauthoritative prior art for the *next* funded attempt — exactly the treatment you give the Python tree in §2.2. You already invented this mechanism; apply it to your own future self.

findings.title: The 15-minute watchdog plus 30-minute turn cap means recovery is a manual forensic exercise at $34/hr burn
findings.detail: Picture the actual 3am: tunnel drops mid-forwarding during a mutating tool call. Per Failure Mode 6, you must not replay automatically. You must 'retain the ambiguity and block until postcondition reconciliation.' So a human — you — now has to inspect the declared postcondition and worktree state, decide whether the write happened, and reconcile. While the meter runs at $34/hr, or you stop the instance and pay $1.37/hr storage against a 6-hour deadline. There is no automation described for reconciliation, only a prohibition on the unsafe automation. The 3am answer to 'can I go back to sleep' is no — and every minute awake costs 57 cents.
findings.evidence: Failure Mode 6: 'Do not replay the mutation automatically; retain the ambiguity and block until postcondition reconciliation or a new reviewed recovery path.' §2.5: 'A stopped instance may retain the staged cache for at most six hours.' Running rate USD 34.0022/hour.
findings.recommendation: Write the reconciliation runbook before you launch, not during the incident. For each mutating tool the Coder can call, pre-declare the postcondition predicate and the exact check command. If you can't enumerate them, you can't reconcile them at 3am. Also: decide *now*, in writing, whether an ambiguous-mutation event at hour 4 of 5 means 'stop and destroy' rather than 'burn the reserve debugging.' Make that decision cold, not tired.

findings.title: You are simultaneously the founder, the Validator, the operator, and the person who has to stay awake
findings.detail: The document assigns roles — founder, Validator, Orchestrator, Coder, Tester, Detector Reviewer, Oracle Curator, named security custodian, named human rights grantor, outcome-blind auditor — with real separation obligations. But this is one person with a $300 budget. The Validator must run first-contact SSH ceremonies, reconcile balance every 60 seconds via monitor, own the append-only ledger, run the contamination scan, operate the egress gate, and be awake for the entire 5-hour warm window because a stopped instance has a 6-hour fuse. There is no described handoff, no second operator, no 'what happens if the Validator human needs to sleep or has an emergency.' The single-point-of-human-failure is not in the threat model.
findings.evidence: §2.3: 'Codex root remains Validator.' §2.5: 'an independent local monitor polls... every 60 seconds.' G-2 owner: Validator. G-3, G-4, G-5, G-9 owner: Validator. §2.4: 'Validator operator' named in the custody residual. No section addresses operator unavailability.
findings.recommendation: Add a failure mode for 'the human Validator becomes unavailable mid-run.' The safe default is almost certainly: monitor detects no operator heartbeat for N minutes → stop instance → (at 6h) destroy. Write it down and implement it, because the alternative is waking up to a drained balance. Also be honest in §5 that role separation here is procedural discipline by one person, not organizational independence — the Oracle Curator being 'organizationally independent of Product/harness authorship' is a claim you cannot currently satisfy.

findings.title: The irreversible disclosure edge has exactly one guard, and it's software you wrote
findings.detail: §0 correctly identifies that a leaked repository byte to a marketplace host is unerasable. The entire defense is a local lineage gate plus byte scanner, plus a forbidden-marker positive control. That's one layer, authored by the same party under time and budget pressure, running in the same process tree as the thing it's guarding. The document acknowledges the residual by writing an 'apology record' — which is honest but is a post-hoc artifact, not a control. Blast radius of a lineage-gate bug: your specifications, your threat model, your store contents, potentially secrets, transmitted to a third-party GPU marketplace host with no attestation, and per your own text, unprovable erasure. That's the one outcome here that isn't just a wasted $300.
findings.evidence: §0: 'Once a repository byte is transmitted to a marketplace host, that disclosure cannot be proven erased even if the instance is destroyed.' §2.2: 'every outbound model request passes a local lineage gate before transmission... then byte-scans as defense in depth.' §2.4: the 'permanent provider_custody_residual... is the apology record for a boundary whose remote half cannot be reconciled.'
findings.recommendation: Add an independent second control that doesn't share a failure mode with the lineage gate: an OS-level egress restriction (the SSH tunnel endpoint as the *only* reachable destination, enforced by firewall/Landlock, not by application code) plus an out-of-process byte tap that logs every outbound body digest to an append-only file the gate cannot write. If the gate has a bug, you want to at least *know* what left, from a source the gate didn't produce. Right now the request census is generated by the same component that decides admission.

findings.title: Fresh Tester, fresh Detector, fresh Curator, fresh pilots — none of this is funded, and it all blocks PROVEN
findings.detail: §2.3 discards the entire prior Factory generation and requires a fresh Tester deriving complete V-1..V-10, a fresh Detector Reviewer, a fresh Oracle Curator, fresh excluded pilots, a power program, and a separately prepaid aggregate measurement ceiling for an eleven-arm experiment with dual calibrated graders. §2.5 explicitly says the $300 'neither funds nor determines V-10 pilot/measurement N.' G-8 is currently *blocked* on a named-human rights grant that doesn't exist. So even in the best case — Coder produces the perfect commit inside 5 hours — you are still blocked at G-8, and G-10/G-11 require an unquantified second budget that could easily be 10-100x the Coder budget. The document never estimates it.
findings.evidence: §2.5: 'It neither funds nor determines V-10 pilot/measurement N... the founder must separately ratify/prepay the complete aggregate coding-and-grading ceiling.' §8: 'G-8 remains blocked on the named-human corpus-rights grant.' §6: 'The named-human auxiliary-corpus rights grant and fresh Detector Review remain blockers.'
findings.recommendation: Before spending the $246, produce a rough order-of-magnitude for the V-10 measurement: eleven arms × N tasks × seeds × (coding model cost + two grader passes). If that number is $50k and you have $300, then the Coder run is buying you a commit you cannot afford to evaluate. That's a legitimate reason to sequence differently: secure the rights grant and a credible measurement budget *first*, because those are hard blockers that no amount of Rust fixes. Also: get the named-human rights grant now. It's free and it's currently a hard stop.

findings.title: Assumption 2 is load-bearing and unvalidated: the safe-Rust OS boundary may not exist
findings.detail: The amendment requires forbid(unsafe_code) in all first-party crates while implementing fexecve/execveat, descriptor enumeration and closing, macOS sandbox_init, and Landlock. The escape hatch is 'the Coder returns FACTORY_QUESTION and stops' — which, in a 5-hour budget, means the run ends with no commit and $200 spent. This is a known-unknown that could be resolved for $0 in an hour of research *before* launching the instance: check whether maintained, pinned, checksummed crates actually expose these primitives behind safe APIs on both macOS and Linux. macOS sandbox_init is deprecated-and-undocumented; that one in particular is a real risk.
findings.evidence: §5 Assumption 2: 'Load-bearing feasibility risk: audited safe Rust dependency APIs can implement the inherited OS boundary while first-party crates forbid unsafe code. If false, implementation blocks for a new architecture decision.' §2.2: 'If the platform boundary cannot be met through audited safe APIs, the Coder returns FACTORY_QUESTION and stops.'
findings.recommendation: Resolve this on your laptop before the instance restarts. Name the specific crates and the specific safe functions for: fexecve/execveat, descriptor enumeration, close-on-exec, Landlock ruleset apply, and macOS sandbox. If any is missing, decide the exception *now* as a cheap amendment rather than discovering it at $34/hr and burning the run on a FACTORY_QUESTION.

findings.title: Single-instance, single-marketplace dependency with no priced fallback
findings.detail: An 8xH200 Vast instance at $34/hr is a spot-market resource. §2.2 says a Vast preemption requires a replacement host to pass 'the full configuration/runtime gates' — which includes re-downloading ~756GB of FP8 weights and rerunning every probe. That's another cold-load charge plus download time, against a reserve of $22.01 that covers exactly one 30-minute turn loss. A single preemption at hour 3 plausibly ends the route. The document treats preemption as a procedural event but never prices it.
findings.evidence: §2.2: 'A Vast preemption during authoring does not create or discard an experiment trial. The Coder thread may resume only after a replacement host receives a new launch record and passes the full configuration/runtime gates.' §2.5 reserve: 'USD 17.01 for one maximum 30-minute Coder turn/cold-prefill loss and USD 5 for shutdown/storage variance.'
findings.recommendation: Price a preemption explicitly: replacement instance acquisition time + 756GB download + full probe suite + cold load. If that number exceeds the $22 reserve (it almost certainly does), then the honest statement is 'a single preemption ends the route as UNFUNDED.' Write that in §3 as a named failure mode so the founder is deciding with eyes open, and consider whether an on-demand/reserved instance at higher hourly rate is actually cheaper in expectation.

findings.title: Gate count vs. budget: G-1 through G-4 must all pass before the clock even starts on useful work
findings.detail: G-4 alone requires: scratch allowlist + positive control, Coder sandbox + descriptor denial probes, lineage-first egress with forbidden-marker positive control, a 60-second spend monitor, a 15-minute checkpoint watchdog, an expanded parser probe matrix (streamed text, required single-tool, tool-output replay, reasoning output, malformed args, endpoint interruption), and mid-forwarding + mutating-tool recovery drills. Several of these require the instance to be warm and running. Every minute of gate execution is $0.57. If G-4 takes 90 minutes of warm-instance time to execute and debug, that's $51 — more than double your entire reserve — consumed before the Coder writes a line.
findings.evidence: G-4 required evidence: 'scratch allowlist/positive control; local Coder sandbox and descriptor denial; lineage-first egress; 60-second spend monitor; 15-minute checkpoint watchdog; expanded parser and mid-forwarding/mutating-tool recovery drills'. §2.5 budget gate reserves only 30 minutes cold-load before the five warm Coder hours.
findings.recommendation: Split the gates by whether they need the paid instance. Build and test everything possible against a cheap local stub or a small model on a $1/hr box: the sandbox, descriptor denial, lineage gate, positive controls, spend monitor, checkpoint watchdog, and recovery drill logic. Only the parser matrix and capacity probes genuinely need the 8xH200. Then add an explicit line item to §2.5: 'gate execution on the warm instance is budgeted at X minutes / $Y' so it isn't silently eating the Coder hours.

findings.title: Failure Mode 10 requires a single clean commit but the recovery design encourages incremental commits
findings.detail: §2.2 says 'The Coder also commits every independently coherent slice' and the watchdog blocks the next turn until a checkpoint exists. G-6 and Failure Mode 10 require 'one clean commit covering every P-1 through P-10 implementation surface.' These are in tension: if the Coder commits incrementally for recovery, what is the terminal single clean commit — a squash? A merge? Who authors it, and does that authoring action itself require a model turn (i.e. money) at the moment the budget is most exhausted? This is exactly the kind of ambiguity that bites at hour 5 with $20 left.
findings.evidence: §2.2: 'The Coder also commits every independently coherent slice.' Failure Mode 10: 'The Coder has no successful terminal state until one clean commit covers every P-1 through P-10 implementation surface and ends FACTORY_STATUS: DONE <sha>.'
findings.recommendation: Define the terminal-commit procedure explicitly and make it cheap: e.g., the incremental commits are the candidate lineage, and the terminal state is a named ref/tag plus the DONE line, requiring no additional model work. Do not leave 'produce the final clean commit' as an unbudgeted model turn.

findings.title: The apology record is well-designed and worth keeping — but note what it implies
findings.detail: The provider_custody_residual is genuinely good practice and rare. Worth naming explicitly: by writing it, you are accepting that the Kinbase specifications and threat model — the crown jewels of this project — will be in the memory of a machine you don't control, with no attestation, and you will never be able to prove otherwise. That's a defensible tradeoff for a proving repository. It would not be defensible if any customer or third-party content were ever in scope. Make sure the founder has said that sentence out loud, not just read it.
findings.evidence: §2.4: 'It is the apology record for a boundary whose remote half cannot be reconciled; it is not stored in Personal, Company, or .kin/, and it cannot be used as evidence that the bytes were erased.'
findings.recommendation: No change to the document. Confirm verbally with the founder that the specifications themselves — not just synthetic probe bytes — leaving to an unattested marketplace host is an accepted, understood cost. If there is any future intent to commercialize on the basis of the specification being proprietary, this decision has a cost you should price now.

persona_reports.summary: **Summary:** This is the most disciplined amendment document I've seen in a while — the falsifiability work in §2.6, the intention-to-treat rules, the apology record, and the refusal to let a green build count as a milestone are all genuinely excellent and rare. That's precisely why the harsh truth matters: the engineering rigor is not the binding constraint here, the money is. You have ~$246 and a five-hour warm window to produce a complete Rust reimplementation of a 29-module system with OS sandboxing, capability separation, and a signed event protocol, all-or-nothing, after seven prior terminations — and even perfect success leaves you blocked at G-8 on an unobtained rights grant and G-10 on an unpriced measurement budget. Before you restart that instance: resolve Assumption 2 on your laptop for free, get the rights grant for free, price the V-10 measurement, and decide whether partial Coder progress is salvageable prior art or genuinely worthless, because the current answer makes every dollar contingent on the last one.

findings.title: The provider balance is an external observation being promoted to a ceiling authority with no owner for the gap
findings.detail: The amendment says 'Vast's account balance is the authority for settled provider spend; the Validator owns a conservative local estimate, never a competing copy of the same fact.' That is the right instinct — but the enforcement rule then says 'Enforcement uses the larger value.' The larger value is a *derived* fact computed from two facts owned by different authorities (Vast's settled balance, the Validator's integrated rate estimate). Nobody owns the derived enforcement number. When the monitor stops inference at USD 285 using the larger value, and Vast later settles at USD 262, there is no named owner of the discrepancy and no statement of who is right. The balance is an input to a calculation, not an entry in a transaction history — but the design treats it as both. Worse: Vast's balance is a *lagging* fact. Provider billing settles asynchronously. The document even acknowledges 'later storage charges' arriving after the observed stop. So at any instant the Validator is comparing a stale authoritative number against a fresh guess, and calling the max 'enforcement.'
findings.evidence: Section 2.5: 'Vast's account balance is the authority for settled provider spend; the Validator owns a conservative local estimate, never a competing copy of the same fact. The estimate is the greater of `initial observed balance - latest balance` and integrated running/stopped rates plus observed one-time charges. Every reconciliation records both numbers, timestamps, and delta. Enforcement uses the larger value.' And: 'Thus staging and qualification had consumed at least USD 53.52 and the balance represented about 7.25 gross full-rate hours before later storage charges.'
findings.recommendation: Name three distinct facts with three distinct owners, and never let them collapse: (1) `provider_settled_spend` — owned by Vast, lagging, immutable once observed, versioned by observation timestamp; (2) `validator_estimated_spend` — owned by the Validator, always a guess, always monotonically increasing; (3) `enforcement_budget_consumed` — owned by the Validator, defined as max(1,2), explicitly labeled a guess in every receipt that carries it. Then state the tolerance: what delta between (1) and (2) is acceptable before the route holds? Right now there is no tolerance, only a max. Add the apology path: when the final settled balance disagrees with the enforcement figure by more than tolerance, which record is amended and who signs it? The document has a founder exception record for *overspend* but none for *underspend caused by an over-conservative estimate that closed the route early as `UNFUNDED`*. That is a real and asymmetric failure: the Validator's guess can deny the founder a funded run, and there is no apology for it.

findings.title: `provider_custody_residual` is a confession, not an apology — no business mechanism attaches to it
findings.detail: You correctly identify that the remote half of the custody boundary cannot be reconciled and you record a permanent residual. That is exactly right in spirit and it is the strongest ownership reasoning in the document. But an apology in my sense is a *business mechanism that runs when the guess was wrong* — a compensating action with a named actor and a trigger. This residual has no trigger and no actor. It records 'the unfalsifiable possibility of provider retention' and then sits there. Nothing happens on any subsequent event. If Vast is breached in 2027 and the Coder prompt bytes surface publicly, what does this record cause to happen? Who is notified? The record names the founder as 'processor authorization' and the Validator as operator, but neither has an obligation attached. Compare the incident-vault HMAC rule in 2.6, which *does* have a real mechanism: destroy the key at 24h, hold requires two named signatures, hold has an `expires_at`, subject erasure destroys immediately. That is an apology path. The custody residual is a memory with no apology.
findings.evidence: Section 2.4: 'It also appends a permanent `provider_custody_residual` ... and the unfalsifiable possibility of provider retention. The residual remains even after a successful destroy. It is the apology record for a boundary whose remote half cannot be reconciled; it is not stored in Personal, Company, or `.kin/`, and it cannot be used as evidence that the bytes were erased.'
findings.recommendation: Do not call it the apology record; it is the *memory* record. Add the actual apology mechanism alongside it: name the disclosure-notification owner, the trigger condition (credible provider breach report, subpoena, or founder request), the recipient set (which is small here — the founder and any named human whose auxiliary-corpus rights grant is in G-8), and the retention horizon for the residual itself. Also state the one thing the residual currently omits: the *byte class inventory* is named, but not a digest list of what actually crossed. The document elsewhere requires 'locally observed request count/digests' — bind those digests into the residual so that a future disclosure can be scoped against what was actually sent rather than what was authorized to be sent. Authorized-class and actually-sent are two different facts with two different owners (policy vs. the egress gate); do not let the residual carry only the first.

findings.title: The deterministic overlay creates an effective artifact that no one owns and that exists only as a derivation
findings.detail: The amendment is explicit that 'There is no rewritten universal specification.' Authority is the base manifest plus this amendment, and the effective artifact is derived by anchor-match-and-replace at read time. This is a clean append-only story for *provenance*. It is a poor story for *ownership at the point of use*. Every consumer — Coder, Tester, Detector, graders, Validator — must independently perform the overlay to know what the rule is. The document requires the Validator to record 'derived effective-artifact digests' in the run binding, which is good, but it does not say the derived artifact is *materialized once by a named owner and thereafter read-only*. If each role re-derives, each role holds a copy of a mutable-by-construction fact, and a mismatch is discovered late (at G-9 combination) rather than at G-1. The stated failure mode `AUTHORITY_MISMATCH` covers a bad anchor, not divergent derivations by different readers.
findings.evidence: Section preamble: 'the effective authority is a deterministic overlay: each exact **old** block below must occur once in the base artifact and is replaced by the paired exact **new** block... The Validator records the base-manifest digest, amendment digest, both amendment ratification receipts, and the derived effective-artifact digests in a new content-addressed run binding. There is no rewritten universal specification and no discretion to choose between readable versions.'
findings.recommendation: Make the derivation happen exactly once, by exactly one owner. At G-1, the Validator materializes the effective artifacts, content-addresses them, and publishes them read-only. Every downstream role reads the *materialized* artifact by digest and never re-runs the overlay. The overlay algorithm remains the audit trail proving how the materialized bytes were produced — that is data on the outside, immutable and versioned — but no consumer branches on it. This also fixes a subtler thing: right now a role could in principle read the base artifact directly and be looking at superseded text with no mechanism to notice. Materialize, digest, distribute the digest, and make reading the base manifest for run purposes a `AUTHORITY_MISMATCH`.

findings.title: Local journal and remote generation are treated as reconcilable, but the reconciliation rule for the ambiguous case is deferred to a human with no bound
findings.detail: The recovery design is strong and I want to say so: 'A host-side generation without a complete local event never happened' is exactly the right ownership statement — the workstation journal is authoritative, the provider's memory is not a source of truth. The `fsync` before and after the tool call, the read-only-replayable / mutating-never-auto-replayed split, all correct. But then failure mode 6 says: 'Do not replay the mutation automatically; retain the ambiguity and block until postcondition reconciliation or a new reviewed recovery path.' That is a block with no owner, no deadline, and no defined outcome set. Under a route that stops inference at USD 285 and destroys the instance at USD 295, an ambiguous mutating call that requires human postcondition reconciliation is a wall-clock event competing against a spend monitor that forcibly cancels turns at 30 minutes. Two authorities — the reconciliation blocker and the spend monitor — can issue contradictory instructions about the same instance, and the precedence between them is unstated.
findings.evidence: Failure mode 6: 'A response/tool interruption produces ambiguous mutation state, duplicate effect, missing completed local event, or a forced fresh thread. Do not replay the mutation automatically; retain the ambiguity and block until postcondition reconciliation or a new reviewed recovery path.' Against section 2.5: 'forcibly cancels a turn at 30 minutes, stops inference at USD 285, and targets provider destruction by USD 295. A monitor failure closes the launch gate and stops the instance.'
findings.recommendation: State the precedence explicitly and name the owner of the ambiguity. Suggest: the spend monitor always wins on the *provider* resource (it may stop and destroy the instance regardless of reconciliation state — the instance is not the ambiguity), while the *worktree* ambiguity is owned by the Validator and blocks only the Coder lane, not the budget lifecycle. Then give the reconciliation a bounded outcome set rather than an open 'reviewed recovery path': the declared postcondition either holds (call completed — record it), demonstrably does not hold (call did not complete — record it), or cannot be determined (record `MUTATION_AMBIGUOUS` against that call ID and the worktree is quarantined at the last checkpoint ref). The third branch is the honest one and it already has the machinery — the 15-minute watchdog checkpoint ref is exactly the recovery point. Say so.

findings.title: The Validator is recorder, budget owner, contamination scanner, gate judge, and appears in nine of eleven gates — the single-owner rule is satisfied by concentration rather than by boundary
findings.detail: Every fact in this design has an owner, and that owner is usually the Validator. G-1 through G-5, G-9, G-11 are Validator-owned; G-2's budget authority, G-3's egress census, G-4's runtime controls, G-5's contamination manifest, and G-9's combination verdict all sit with the same actor. The role separations that *are* enforced are the right ones (Coder cannot read tests, Tester cannot read implementation, Detector is implementation-blind, Curator is schema-blind and organizationally independent). But the Validator has no counterparty on any fact it owns. Section 2.4 correctly rejects putting Factory receipts in the Company store as 'circular proof' — 'the Validator ledger exists before the Product and cannot be made trustworthy by the component it is judging.' The same argument applies one level up: the Validator ledger is judged by the Validator. There is no named mechanism by which a Validator recording error is detected. This is not a theoretical concern — it crosses a real boundary, because the run ledger is the only record of whether pre-ratification egress ever carried a repository byte (G-3), and G-3's failure disposition is 'unauthorized send blocks route permanently.'
findings.evidence: Section 2.4: 'Run-control receipts ... live in the Validator-owned, append-only Factory run ledger outside author lanes ... names the Validator as recorder ... Git/content digests establish byte integrity; no actor-authentication signature is claimed unless actually present.' And G-3: 'complete local request census for prior synthetic probes and no known repo-derived request; any uncertainty stated, never upgraded to proof.'
findings.recommendation: You do not need a second Validator. You need one fact with a second owner: make the *egress proxy's* local request receipt an independently-owned artifact. The proxy already 'records the digest and byte count of every outbound body before forwarding' — have it write to an append-only log the Validator can read but not rewrite (separate uid, append-only file attribute, or simply a separate signed chain). Then G-3's census is a reconciliation between two owners rather than an assertion by one, and a Validator recording gap becomes *detectable* as a delta instead of invisible. This is cheap and it converts the strongest irreversible claim in the document from a memory into a reconciled fact. Note the document already admits the weakness: 'no actor-authentication signature is claimed unless actually present.' Make it present for this one fact.

findings.title: Prefix cache is correctly classified as provider-owned transient state, but the classification is asserted rather than enforced
findings.detail: This is one of the better ownership calls in the document: 'prefix caching is permitted because repo-derived prefixes are transient memory inside the explicitly authorized Coder processor boundary after ratification. It is volatile provider state, not public-only state, not a result journal, not recovery evidence, and not part of any correctness claim.' Correct on every count. The problem is that the enforcement is a configuration flag — 'persistent prefix/request caches are disabled' — set on a host owned by someone else, and the document elsewhere states plainly that 'container isolation is not a confidentiality proof' and 'these controls do not exclude the host operator.' So the classification 'volatile' is a guess about a system you do not control, and the guess has no apology path. If the prefix cache turns out to have been persisted (host operator, vLLM bug, swap despite the flag), what changes? Nothing in the document. The `provider_custody_residual` names byte classes but does not distinguish 'bytes we sent' from 'bytes the provider may have retained in derived form.'
findings.evidence: Section 2.2: 'prefix caching is permitted because repo-derived prefixes are transient memory inside the explicitly authorized Coder processor boundary after ratification. It is volatile provider state...' against section 2.4: 'The host operator can technically access host files and memory; container isolation is not a confidentiality proof' and 'Request and access logging, swap, CPU offload, and persistent prefix/request caches are disabled. These settings reduce accidental inference-server persistence; they do not protect against the host operator.'
findings.recommendation: You have already done the hard reasoning — just close the loop. State the tolerance explicitly: 'prefix cache contents are assumed volatile; this assumption is unverifiable and is subsumed by the provider_custody_residual.' Then add prefix-derived state to the residual's named byte classes so that a future disclosure scoping does not have to argue about whether cached prefixes count. One sentence. It costs nothing and it means the guess and the apology point at the same record.

findings.title: The historical Python snapshot has a manifest owner but its exclusion from the candidate has no enforcement owner
findings.detail: G-5 gives the Validator ownership of the read-only path/digest manifest, with a denial positive control — good, that is a real capability boundary rather than an instruction. But the downstream rule is: 'No prior file may enter the Rust product commit, evidence packet, or proof claim except its manifest digest and this provenance statement.' Who checks that at G-6? The Coder handoff evidence is 'one clean Rust commit ... full status/diff receipt, terminal FACTORY_STATUS: DONE <sha>.' Nothing in G-6 verifies that no manifested prior file content appears in the commit. Failure mode 8 says 'The old Python tree ... appears in the Rust candidate. Deny the whole historical snapshot or reject the candidate' — but that is a disposition without a detector. Compare this to how carefully the *test-leakage* case is handled: 'A pre-combination leakage control compares Coder-visible bytes with hidden test/oracle-only markers.' Prior-art leakage gets no equivalent mechanical control, only an instruction to the model.
findings.evidence: Section 2.2: 'No prior file may enter the Rust product commit, evidence packet, or proof claim except its manifest digest and this provenance statement.' G-6 required evidence: 'one clean Rust commit covering every P-1 through P-10 implementation surface, full status/diff receipt, terminal `FACTORY_STATUS: DONE <sha>`.' Failure mode 8 names the outcome but no gate detects it.
findings.recommendation: Add to G-6's required evidence a mechanical check owned by the Validator: for every path/digest in the G-5 manifest, assert absence of that content (and of near-duplicate content above a stated similarity threshold) in the candidate commit. State the threshold before the Coder runs, and state the disposition on a hit. Note the honest complication: the Coder is *allowed* to read the prior art, so identical short lines will legitimately recur. Pick the tolerance now, before you have a candidate — otherwise the threshold gets chosen after you see the diff, which is exactly the pattern section 2.6 is written to prevent elsewhere.

findings.title: Founder approvals are 'verbatim conversation-derived receipts' — an authorization fact whose authority rests on the recorder
findings.detail: The document is admirably honest here: 'Founder approvals are retained as verbatim conversation-derived receipts with that limitation.' The limitation being that Git/content digests establish byte integrity but no actor authentication is claimed. So the highest-precedence authority in the whole system — the founder's ratification, which G-1 requires before any author dispatch — is a fact recorded by the Validator about the founder, with no artifact owned by the founder. The Validator is trusted to have transcribed correctly. For a decision the document itself classifies as Type 1 / expensive-to-revert / irreversible-disclosure-edge, that is a thin authority chain.
findings.evidence: Section 2.4: 'Founder approvals are retained as verbatim conversation-derived receipts with that limitation. These records cannot self-ratify Product facts.' G-1 required evidence: 'exact amendment digest receipts.'
findings.recommendation: For G-1 and G-2 specifically — ratification and processor authorization, the two decisions with irreversible edges — require an artifact the founder owns, not one the Validator transcribes. A signed commit, a signed digest, or at minimum a founder-authored file containing the exact amendment SHA-256 in the founder's own hand. The document already requires 'both amendment ratification receipts,' implying two parties; make the founder's half founder-owned. For lower-stakes approvals, the current honest limitation is fine and I would not add ceremony.

findings.title: The six-hour stopped-cache deadline has no owner for the clock and no apology for a false expiry
findings.detail: 'A stopped instance may retain the staged cache for at most six hours while ratification or bounded recovery is active; at that deadline the Validator restarts only if all gates admit, otherwise destroys it and reports that a future host must restage.' The clock is real and the disposition is clean. But the deadline is measured against provider-side state (instance stopped-at time) reconciled against local Validator time, and a destroy is irreversible — restaging is the 755.7 GB download plus USD 17.01 cold-load allowance. If the clock is wrong by a few minutes in the conservative direction, the route pays a real, quantified penalty. There is no record of the destroy-vs-restart decision inputs, so a wrongly-early destroy is indistinguishable from a correctly-timed one after the fact.
findings.evidence: Section 2.5: 'A stopped instance may retain the staged cache for at most six hours while ratification or bounded recovery is active; at that deadline the Validator restarts only if all gates admit, otherwise destroys it and reports that a future host must restage. Stopping is not terminal cleanup.'
findings.recommendation: Make the destroy decision a ledger record with its inputs: observed provider stopped-at timestamp, local clock, computed elapsed, gate states at decision time, and the resulting disposition. It costs one record and it means a restage cost is attributable rather than mysterious. Given that everything else in this document is content-addressed and receipted, this decision standing outside the ledger is an inconsistency more than a risk.

persona_reports.summary:
I'll review this as Pat Helland, focused on ownership boundaries, reconciliation, and the treatment of external facts.



## Summary

This is unusually disciplined work on ownership — better than most production systems I have reviewed. The document gets the hardest things right: the workstation journal is authoritative over provider memory ("a host-side generation without a complete local event never happened"), infrastructure receipts are explicitly *not* Product evidence, prefix caches are correctly classified as transient provider state rather than a result journal, and putting Factory receipts into the Company store is rejected as circular proof. The distinction between "Vast's balance is authoritative for settled spend" and "the Validator owns an estimate, never a competing copy" is exactly the right framing.

My findings cluster on two gaps. First, several facts are correctly identified as guesses but have no apology path attached — the `provider_custody_residual` is a memory with no mechanism, the prefix-cache volatility claim has no fallback if false, and an over-conservative budget estimate can deny a funded run with no exception record (the overspend case has one; the underspend case does not). Second, the Validator owns nearly every fact with no counterparty, which is defensible for most of them but not for the pre-ratification egress census, where the failure disposition is permanent route denial and the only witness is the actor being witnessed — the egress proxy already produces an independent receipt, so making it independently *owned* is cheap and closes the strongest irreversible claim in the document.

finding_a.title: The 15-minute checkpoint watchdog and the 30-minute maximum turn are in direct conflict
finding_a.detail: §2.2 requires 'a Validator watchdog snapshots dirty work at least every fifteen minutes' and 'A missed watchdog interval blocks the next model turn until a checkpoint is made.' §2.5 requires the monitor to 'forcibly cancel a turn at 30 minutes.' A single model turn can therefore legally run 30 minutes, during which two watchdog intervals elapse. The watchdog snapshots 'dirty work' using a private temporary Git index — but during an in-flight turn the Coder's tools may be mid-write. The amendment does not say whether the watchdog can snapshot while a mutating tool call is in flight. If it can, it may capture a torn intermediate state and fsync it as a checkpoint ref — which §2.2 elsewhere treats as recovery evidence. If it cannot, then a 30-minute turn containing a long mutating call necessarily misses its interval, which 'blocks the next model turn' — producing a deadlock: the turn cannot complete because it is blocked, and the checkpoint cannot be made because a mutation is in flight. Neither branch is addressed.
finding_a.evidence: §2.2: 'a Validator watchdog snapshots dirty work at least every fifteen minutes ... A missed watchdog interval blocks the next model turn until a checkpoint is made; it is not left to model discipline.' §2.5: 'forcibly cancels a turn at 30 minutes.'
finding_a.recommendation: State the interaction explicitly: either the watchdog quiesces mutating tool calls before snapshotting (and the 15-minute clock pauses during a quiesce), or checkpoints taken during in-flight mutation are marked `torn` and are explicitly not valid recovery bases. Define the deadlock resolution when a mutating call outlives the watchdog interval.

finding_b.title: The 15-minute checkpoint watchdog and the 30-minute forced turn cancellation can deadlock a long turn
finding_b.detail: The spend monitor 'forcibly cancels a turn at 30 minutes'. The watchdog requires a checkpoint every 15 minutes and 'a missed watchdog interval blocks the next model turn until a checkpoint is made'. A single model turn that runs 25 minutes will cross one watchdog interval with the Coder mid-generation and no new commit; the watchdog snapshots dirty work via a private temp index, which is fine, but the interaction between 'blocks the next model turn' and 'forcibly cancels at 30 minutes' is unspecified when the cancellation itself is what produces the dirty state. Minor, but it is a live-lock shape in a system where each blocked minute costs USD 0.57.
finding_b.evidence: "a Validator watchdog snapshots dirty work at least every fifteen minutes ... A missed watchdog interval blocks the next model turn until a checkpoint is made" and "forcibly cancels a turn at 30 minutes"
finding_b.recommendation: State the precedence explicitly: the watchdog snapshot is non-blocking and runs concurrently with an in-flight turn; only a *failed* snapshot blocks the next turn. And state that a forced 30-minute cancellation always triggers an immediate snapshot before the block is evaluated.

disagreements.tension: Adversarial rates this high, but Subject Matter Expert rates it low. The gap suggests different risk models worth examining.
